candidate_source_and_statement.candidate_natural_language_statement: Prove that the sum of n squares can be found as follows: 1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + ... + n^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
candidate_source_and_statement.original_source_statement: Prove that the sum of n squares can be found as follows: 1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + ... + n^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
candidate_source_and_statement.source_citation: Oscar Levin, Discrete Mathematics: An Open Introduction, 3rd edition, section 2.5, exercise 10 (online text).
candidate_source_and_statement.source_location: Section 2.5, Exercises, item 10; publisher page lines 911–914.
candidate_source_and_statement.required_attribution: Oscar Levin, Discrete Mathematics: An Open Introduction, 3rd ed., §2.5, Exercise 10 (DMOI3-section-2.5-exercise-10); CC BY-SA 4.0; https://discrete.openmathbooks.org/dmoi3.html
candidate_source_and_statement.adaptation_history: Represented the sum from 1 through n by a Finset sum over 0 through n; the added zero term is 0. The right side uses natural-number division by 6.

proposed_formalization.lean_statement: theorem sum_squares_closed_form (n : ℕ) : (∑ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), k ^ 2) = n * (n + 1) * (2 * n + 1) / 6
